title: Vector Calculus

sources.title: Faculty of Mathematics, University of Cambridge: Schedules of Lecture Courses and Form of Examinations, Mathematical Tripos 2026-27
sources.used_for: syllabus (schedule sections, topic order, lecture counts, starred material) and Part IA examination format; the 'Integration in R² and R³' section is split here into line integrals and surface/volume integrals

about: Vector Calculus is a 24-lecture Lent Term course in Part IA of the Cambridge Mathematical Tripos. Following the official schedule it covers curves in R³, line, surface and volume integrals with change of variables, the operators grad, div and curl, the divergence, Green's and Stokes's theorems (with applications to fluids and Maxwell's equations), Laplace's and Poisson's equations, and Cartesian tensors. General orthogonal curvilinear coordinates are starred, so not examinable. It is examined on Paper 3 alongside Groups; each Part IA paper has a Section I of shorter questions and a Section II of longer ones.
topics: Curves in R³: arc length, curvature and torsion
Surface and volume integrals; change of variables
Vector operators: grad, div, curl and identities
Integration theorems: divergence, Green's and Stokes's

notes.h: Curves in R³: arc length, curvature and torsion
notes.body:
The course opens with a single lecture on the geometry of curves. It is short in the schedule, but the calculations (often for a helix-like curve) are quick to practise.

Parametrised curves and arc length
- A curve is given by r(t) for t in an interval, with r′(t) ≠ 0 (a regular parametrisation).
- Arc length from t₀: s(t) = ∫ |r′(u)| du from t₀ to t, so ds/dt = |r′(t)|.
- Using s as the parameter gives unit speed: |dr/ds| = 1.

The Frenet frame
- Unit tangent: t̂ = dr/ds = r′/|r′|.
- Since t̂·t̂ = 1, differentiating gives t̂·(dt̂/ds) = 0, so dt̂/ds is perpendicular to t̂. Write dt̂/ds = κn̂ with κ ≥ 0 the curvature and n̂ the unit principal normal (defined where κ > 0).
- Binormal: b̂ = t̂ × n̂. Then (t̂, n̂, b̂) is a right-handed orthonormal frame moving along the curve.
- Torsion τ is defined by db̂/ds = −τn̂. This minus sign is a convention: it is the common one, but some books use db̂/ds = +τn̂, which flips the sign of τ (and of the τ terms below). It measures how fast the curve twists out of its osculating plane (the plane of t̂ and n̂). A plane curve has τ = 0.
- Frenet–Serret equations: dt̂/ds = κn̂, dn̂/ds = −κt̂ + τb̂, db̂/ds = −τn̂.
- Radius of curvature: ρ = 1/κ. A circle of radius a has κ = 1/a; a straight line has κ = 0.

Formulae with any parameter
- κ = |r′ × r″| / |r′|³.
- τ = (r′ × r″)·r‴ / |r′ × r″|².
These are quicker in exams than reparametrising by arc length, but the schedule's definitions are via s, so be ready to derive things from them.

Worked example: the helix
r(t) = (a cos t, a sin t, bt), a > 0.
- r′ = (−a sin t, a cos t, b), |r′| = √(a² + b²) = c, so s = ct.
- t̂ = (−a sin t, a cos t, b)/c.
- dt̂/ds = (1/c) dt̂/dt = (−a cos t, −a sin t, 0)/c². So κ = a/(a² + b²) and n̂ = (−cos t, −sin t, 0), pointing horizontally towards the axis.
- b̂ = t̂ × n̂ = (b sin t, −b cos t, a)/c.
- db̂/ds = (b cos t, b sin t, 0)/c² = −(b/c²)n̂, so τ = b/(a² + b²).
- Check limits: b = 0 gives a circle (κ = 1/a, τ = 0); with a = 3, b = 4 we get κ = 3/25 and τ = 4/25.

Exam tips: state your sign convention for torsion (here db̂/ds = −τn̂; use whatever convention the question or your lecture notes fix); check κ ≥ 0, that t̂, n̂, b̂ are unit and orthogonal, and that your answer gives sensible limits.

Line integrals are the first of the integrals in the "Integration in R² and R³" section. They lead directly to conservative fields and potentials (in the schedule, conservative fields and scalar potentials are listed under vector operators, so they are grouped here for convenience).

Definitions
- For a scalar field f and curve C given by r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b: ∫_C f ds = ∫ f(r(t)) |r′(t)| dt. With f = 1 this is the length of C. It does not depend on the direction of travel.
- For a vector field F: ∫_C F·dr = ∫ F(r(t))·r′(t) dt from a to b. Reversing the direction changes the sign. Physically, it is the work done by the force F along C.
- In components: ∫_C (F₁ dx + F₂ dy + F₃ dz).
- A closed curve integral is written ∮_C F·dr; it is called the circulation of F round C.

Worked example (path dependence)
F = (xy, x, 0) from (0, 0, 0) to (1, 1, 0).
- Along r = (t, t², 0): F·r′ = (t³)(1) + (t)(2t) = t³ + 2t², integral 1/4 + 2/3 = 11/12.
- Along the straight line r = (t, t, 0): F·r′ = t² + t, integral 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6.
- Different answers, so F is not conservative. Consistently, ∇ × F = (0, 0, 1 − x) ≠ 0.

Conservative fields
The following are equivalent for a continuous field F on a connected open region D:
- F is conservative: F = ∇φ for some scalar potential φ.
- ∫_C F·dr depends only on the end points of C.
- ∮_C F·dr = 0 for every closed curve C in D.
If F = ∇φ, then ∫_C F·dr = φ(end) − φ(start), since d(φ(r(t)))/dt = ∇φ·r′.

Testing and finding potentials
- If F = ∇φ then ∇ × F = 0. Conversely, if F is continuously differentiable with ∇ × F = 0 on a simply connected open region (every loop can be shrunk to a point) then F is conservative.
- Simple connectedness matters: F = (−y, x, 0)/(x² + y²) has zero curl away from the z-axis, but its circulation round the unit circle is 2π.
- To find φ, integrate component by component. Example: F = (2xy + z, x², x). ∇ × F = 0. From ∂φ/∂x = 2xy + z, φ = x²y + xz + g(y, z); ∂φ/∂y = x² forces g independent of y; ∂φ/∂z = x forces g constant. So φ = x²y + xz, and the work from (0, 0, 0) to (1, 2, 3) is φ(1, 2, 3) − φ(0, 0, 0) = 2 + 3 = 5.

Exact differentials
- F·dr = F₁dx + F₂dy + F₃dz is exact if it equals dφ; this is the same as F being conservative.

Exam tips: always state the parametrisation and its range and compute r′ explicitly; for "show that F is conservative", check the curl and then exhibit φ, and say why the region allows you to conclude.

notes.h: Surface and volume integrals; change of variables
notes.body:
This part of the schedule covers integrals over surfaces and volumes, in Cartesian, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, and the change of variables formula.

Change of variables
- For a map (u, v) ↦ (x, y), dx dy = |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| du dv, where the Jacobian ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) is the determinant of the matrix of partial derivatives.
- Plane polars: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ give dx dy = r dr dθ.
- Cylindrical polars (ρ, φ, z): dV = ρ dρ dφ dz.
- Spherical polars (r, θ, φ) with x = r sin θ cos φ, y = r sin θ sin φ, z = r cos θ: dV = r² sin θ dr dθ dφ, for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π and 0 ≤ φ < 2π.
- Example: I = ∫ e^(−x²) dx over ℝ. I² = ∬ e^(−(x²+y²)) dx dy = ∫∫ e^(−r²) r dr dθ = 2π × 1/2 = π, so I = √π.

Volume integrals
- ∫_V f dV, computed as a triple integral with limits that describe V.
- Example: for the solid hemisphere r ≤ a, z ≥ 0, ∫ z dV = ∫∫∫ (r cos θ) r² sin θ dr dθ dφ = 2π × (a⁴/4) × (1/2) = πa⁴/4. As the volume is 2πa³/3, the centroid is at height 3a/8.

Surfaces and surface integrals
- A surface parametrised by r(u, v) has tangent vectors r_u and r_v. The vector area element is dS = (r_u × r_v) du dv (choose the order to match the orientation you want), and the scalar area element is dS = |r_u × r_v| du dv.
- Sphere of radius a: dS = a² sin θ dθ dφ, with unit outward normal n̂ = r/a. Cylinder of radius a: dS = a dφ dz, n̂ = ρ̂.
- For a surface z = h(x, y): dS = (−h_x, −h_y, 1) dx dy (upward normal).
- Flux of F through S: ∫_S F·dS = ∫_S F·n̂ dS. Example: F = r through a sphere of radius a: F·n̂ = a everywhere, so the flux is a × 4πa² = 4πa³.
- Example: F = (0, 0, z) through the curved hemisphere r = a, z ≥ 0, outward. F·n̂ = z cos θ = a cos²θ, so the flux is ∫∫ a cos²θ · a² sin θ dθ dφ = 2πa³ × 1/3 = 2πa³/3 (θ from 0 to π/2).

Orientation
- A surface integral of a vector field needs an orientation (a continuous choice of unit normal). For a closed surface, the convention is the outward normal.
- Reversing the orientation changes the sign of the flux.

Exam tips: draw the region and write the limits before integrating; in spherical polars do not forget the r² sin θ, and check by integrating 1 (e.g. you should recover 4πa³/3 or 4πa²).

notes.h: Vector operators: grad, div, curl and identities
notes.body:
This five-lecture block introduces the differential operators of vector calculus. Fluency with suffix notation (from Vectors and Matrices) is essential here.

Gradient and directional derivatives
- For a scalar field f, ∇f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y, ∂f/∂z). The rate of change of f in the direction of a unit vector û is û·∇f.
- So f increases fastest in the direction of ∇f, at rate |∇f|, and ∇f is normal to the level surfaces f = constant.
- Example: f = x²y + z³ at (1, 2, −1). ∇f = (2xy, x², 3z²) = (4, 1, 3). In the direction (2, −1, 2)/3 the rate of change is (8 − 1 + 6)/3 = 13/3. The tangent plane to the level surface there is 4x + y + 3z = 3.

Divergence, curl and the Laplacian (Cartesian)
- ∇·F = ∂Fᵢ/∂xᵢ (summed). (∇ × F)ᵢ = εᵢⱼₖ ∂Fₖ/∂xⱼ. ∇²f = ∇·∇f = ∂²f/∂xᵢ∂xᵢ.
- Standard results, with r = |r|: ∇·r = 3, ∇ × r = 0, ∇r = r/r, ∇(1/r) = −r/r³, ∇·(r/r³) = 0 and ∇²(1/r) = 0 for r ≠ 0. More generally ∇(f(r)) = f′(r) r/r.
- F is irrotational if ∇ × F = 0, solenoidal if ∇·F = 0, and conservative if F = ∇φ.

Identities (prove them with suffix notation)
- ∇ × (∇f) = 0 and ∇·(∇ × F) = 0, because εᵢⱼₖ is antisymmetric while second partial derivatives are symmetric.
- ∇·(fF) = f∇·F + F·∇f, and ∇ × (fF) = f∇ × F + ∇f × F.
- ∇·(F × G) = G·(∇ × F) − F·(∇ × G).
- ∇ × (∇ × F) = ∇(∇·F) − ∇²F, using εᵢⱼₖεₖₗₘ = δᵢₗδⱼₘ − δᵢₘδⱼₗ.
- ∇ × (F × G) = F(∇·G) − G(∇·F) + (G·∇)F − (F·∇)G.
- Proof sketch for ∇·(F × G): ∂ᵢ(εᵢⱼₖFⱼGₖ) = εᵢⱼₖ(∂ᵢFⱼ)Gₖ + εᵢⱼₖFⱼ(∂ᵢGₖ) = Gₖ(εₖᵢⱼ∂ᵢFⱼ) − Fⱼ(εⱼᵢₖ∂ᵢGₖ), which is G·(∇ × F) − F·(∇ × G).

Potentials
- On a simply connected region, ∇ × F = 0 implies F = ∇φ. On a suitable region (e.g. all of R³), ∇·F = 0 implies F = ∇ × A for a vector potential A, which is not unique (A + ∇χ works too).

Cylindrical and spherical coordinates
The schedule gives these formulae as statement only for cylindrical and spherical coordinates; the extension to general orthogonal curvilinear coordinates is starred, so non-examinable.
- Cylindrical (ρ, φ, z): ∇f = (∂f/∂ρ)ρ̂ + (1/ρ)(∂f/∂φ)φ̂ + (∂f/∂z)ẑ; ∇²f = (1/ρ)∂(ρ ∂f/∂ρ)/∂ρ + (1/ρ²)∂²f/∂φ² + ∂²f/∂z².
- Spherical (r, θ, φ): ∇f = (∂f/∂r)r̂ + (1/r)(∂f/∂θ)θ̂ + (1/(r sin θ))(∂f/∂φ)φ̂; for f = f(r), ∇²f = (1/r²) d(r² df/dr)/dr. For F = F(r) r̂, ∇·F = (1/r²) d(r²F)/dr.
- The unit vectors ρ̂, φ̂, r̂, θ̂ vary with position, so you cannot differentiate components naively.

Exam tips: in suffix notation proofs, write every index, check free indices match on both sides, and quote the ε–δ identity explicitly.

notes.h: Integration theorems: divergence, Green's and Stokes's
notes.body:
The five lectures on integration theorems are the heart of the course. A typical long question asks you to state a theorem precisely and verify it, or to use it to evaluate something awkward.

The theorems
- In each theorem below F (or P, Q, φ, ψ) is assumed continuously differentiable (twice, for φ and ψ in Green's second theorem) on a region containing V, A or S and its boundary.
- Divergence theorem: for a bounded volume V with closed, piecewise smooth boundary S and outward normal, ∫_V ∇·F dV = ∫_S F·dS.
- Green's theorem in the plane: for a region A in the plane with boundary C traversed anticlockwise, ∮_C (P dx + Q dy) = ∬_A (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dx dy.
- Stokes's theorem: for an oriented surface S with boundary curve C, ∫_S (∇ × F)·dS = ∮_C F·dr. The orientation of C and the normal of S must agree by the right-hand rule.
- Green's second theorem: ∫_V (φ∇²ψ − ψ∇²φ) dV = ∫_S (φ∇ψ − ψ∇φ)·dS. It follows from the divergence theorem applied to φ∇ψ − ψ∇φ. (Green's first identity, ∫_V (φ∇²ψ + ∇φ·∇ψ) dV = ∫_S φ∇ψ·dS, is the version used for uniqueness proofs.)
- Green's theorem in the plane is Stokes's theorem for a flat surface with F = (P, Q, 0).

Interpretations
- Taking a small volume δV around a point, ∇·F ≈ (1/δV)∫ F·dS: divergence is outward flux per unit volume.
- Similarly n̂·(∇ × F) is the circulation per unit area round a small loop with normal n̂.

Worked examples
- Area by Green: with P = −y/2, Q = x/2, area = (1/2)∮(x dy − y dx). For the ellipse x = a cos t, y = b sin t this gives (1/2)∫ ab dt = πab.
- Stokes check: F = (−y, x, 0), ∇ × F = (0, 0, 2). For a disc of radius a in the plane z = 0 (normal +z), the surface integral is 2πa², and the circle integral is ∫ (a² sin²t + a² cos²t) dt = 2πa².
- Divergence check: F = (0, 0, z) over the solid hemisphere r ≤ a, z ≥ 0. ∇·F = 1, so the volume integral is 2πa³/3. The flat base has z = 0, so contributes 0, and the curved surface gives 2πa³/3 (see the surface integral note).
- For any closed S bounding V, ∫_S r·dS = 3 × volume of V, because ∇·r = 3.

Applications in the schedule
- Conservation laws: if ρ is a density and J its flux, conservation in every volume gives ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J = 0. For a fluid, J = ρu.
- Gauss's law: ∫_S E·dS = Q/ε₀ is equivalent, by the divergence theorem, to ∇·E = ρ/ε₀.
- Maxwell's equations (statement): ∇·E = ρ/ε₀, ∇·B = 0, ∇ × E = −∂B/∂t, ∇ × B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t. Taking the divergence of the last and using the first gives charge conservation ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J = 0.

Exam tips: when verifying a theorem, compute both sides separately and include every piece of the boundary (flat bases, ends of cylinders); state orientations explicitly.

Laplace's equation ∇²φ = 0 governs steady temperatures, electrostatic potentials in empty space and ideal fluid flow. Poisson's equation ∇²φ = f adds a source. This four-lecture block uses the integration theorems to prove things about them.

Basic solutions
- Solutions of Laplace's equation are called harmonic functions.
- Spherically symmetric solutions in R³: (1/r²)(r²φ′)′ = 0 gives φ = A + B/r.
- Cylindrically symmetric (or radial in R²): (1/ρ)(ρφ′)′ = 0 gives φ = A + B ln ρ.
- Example: φ harmonic in a < r < b with φ = V on r = a and φ = 0 on r = b. Solving A + B/a = V, A + B/b = 0 gives φ = Va(b − r)/(r(b − a)).

Uniqueness
- Dirichlet problem: ∇²φ = f in V with φ given on the boundary S. The solution is unique.
- Neumann problem: ∇²φ = f in V with ∂φ/∂n = n̂·∇φ given on S. The solution is unique up to an added constant (and a solution can only exist if ∫_V f dV = ∫_S (∂φ/∂n) dS).
- Proof: let ψ = φ₁ − φ₂, so ∇²ψ = 0 in V. Apply the divergence theorem to ψ∇ψ: ∫_V |∇ψ|² dV = ∫_S ψ ∂ψ/∂n dS − ∫_V ψ∇²ψ dV = 0, since either ψ = 0 or ∂ψ/∂n = 0 on S. As |∇ψ|² ≥ 0 and is continuous, ∇ψ = 0, so ψ is constant; with Dirichlet data the constant is 0.

Maximum principle
- A function harmonic in a bounded region and continuous up to its boundary attains its maximum (and minimum) on the boundary; if the region is connected, it cannot have an interior maximum or minimum unless it is constant.
- Idea: harmonic functions have the mean value property, φ at a point equals its average over any sphere centred there inside the region, so an interior maximum would force φ to be constant nearby.
- Consequence: steady temperatures have no interior hot spots, and an electrostatic potential in empty space has no interior maximum or minimum.

Gauss's method for symmetric sources
- For gravity, g = −∇φ with ∇²φ = 4πGρ. Integrate over a ball of radius r and use the divergence theorem: ∫_S g·dS = −4πG M(r), where M(r) is the mass inside.
- Spherical symmetry: g = g(r) r̂, so 4πr² g(r) = −4πG M(r), i.e. g = −G M(r)/r² r̂. Outside a spherically symmetric body of mass M, the field is that of a point mass.
- Example: uniform density ρ₀ in r < a. Inside, M(r) = (4/3)πρ₀r³, so g = −(4/3)πGρ₀ r r̂, growing linearly with r.
- Cylindrical symmetry works the same way with a cylinder of radius ρ and length L: 2πρL g(ρ) = −4πG × (mass per unit length × L).

Poisson's equation as an integral
- ∇²(1/r) = 0 for r ≠ 0, but ∫ ∇·∇(1/r) dV over any ball centred at 0 equals the flux of −r/r³ through its surface, which is −4π. Hence ∇²(1/r) acts like −4πδ.
- The solution of ∇²φ = f decaying at infinity is φ(r) = −(1/4π) ∫ f(r′)/|r − r′| dV′. For gravity this gives φ = −G ∫ ρ(r′)/|r − r′| dV′.

Exam tips: for uniqueness, name which identity you use and say exactly where the boundary term vanishes; in Gauss's method, state the symmetry assumption that lets you take g outside the integral.

The final five lectures introduce Cartesian tensors: objects whose components transform in a fixed way under a rotation of axes. The course emphasises second-rank tensors.

Transformation laws
- Rotate to new orthonormal axes. Coordinates transform by x′ᵢ = Rᵢⱼxⱼ, where R is orthogonal (RRᵀ = I) and, for a rotation, det R = 1.
- A scalar is unchanged. A vector satisfies v′ᵢ = Rᵢⱼvⱼ. A tensor of rank n satisfies T′ᵢⱼ...ₖ = RᵢₚRⱼₛ...RₖᵣTₚₛ...ᵣ, one factor of R for each index.
- Example: ∂²f/∂xᵢ∂xⱼ is a rank-2 tensor; the outer product uᵢvⱼ of two vectors is a rank-2 tensor.

Algebra of tensors
- Tensors of the same rank can be added; the product of a rank-m and a rank-n tensor is a rank-(m + n) tensor.
- Contraction (setting two indices equal and summing) lowers the rank by 2. For example Tᵢᵢ (the trace) is a scalar and Tᵢⱼvⱼ is a vector.
- A rank-2 tensor splits uniquely into symmetric and antisymmetric parts: Tᵢⱼ = (Tᵢⱼ + Tⱼᵢ)/2 + (Tᵢⱼ − Tⱼᵢ)/2. Symmetry is preserved under rotation.
- An antisymmetric rank-2 tensor has 3 independent components and corresponds to a vector ω via Aᵢⱼ = εᵢⱼₖωₖ.

Isotropic tensors
- A tensor is isotropic if its components are the same in every rotated frame.
- Every isotropic rank-2 tensor is λδᵢⱼ; every isotropic rank-3 tensor is λεᵢⱼₖ.
- (For reference, rank 4: αδᵢⱼδₖₗ + βδᵢₖδⱼₗ + γδᵢₗδⱼₖ.)
- Use: integrals over spheres or balls. ∫ xᵢxⱼ dV over the ball r ≤ a must be isotropic, so it equals λδᵢⱼ. Taking the trace, 3λ = ∫ r² dV = 4πa⁵/5, so λ = 4πa⁵/15.

Principal axes
- A real symmetric rank-2 tensor can be diagonalised by a rotation (revision from Vectors and Matrices): there is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, the principal axes, with real eigenvalues, the principal values.

Physical examples
- Inertia tensor of a body of density ρ: Iᵢⱼ = ∫ ρ(r²δᵢⱼ − xᵢxⱼ) dV, giving angular momentum Lᵢ = Iᵢⱼωⱼ. For a uniform solid sphere of mass M and radius a, using the integral above, Iᵢⱼ = ρ(4πa⁵/5 − 4πa⁵/15)δᵢⱼ = (2/5)Ma²δᵢⱼ.
- Conductivity: in an anisotropic material, Jᵢ = σᵢⱼEⱼ. The current need not be parallel to E unless E lies along a principal axis.

Quotient theorem
- If Tᵢⱼvⱼ is a vector for every vector v, then Tᵢⱼ is a rank-2 tensor. More generally, if contracting an array with an arbitrary tensor always gives a tensor, the array is itself a tensor.
- This is how one shows σᵢⱼ and Iᵢⱼ are tensors: J and E (or L and ω) are vectors, and E (or ω) is arbitrary.

Exam tips: when asked to show something is a tensor, write out the transformation of each factor explicitly; when using isotropy, say why the integral is isotropic (the region is symmetric under all rotations).

Normal to the level surfaces of f, pointing towards increasing f, with magnitude equal to the maximum rate of increase.
(∇ × F)ᵢ = εᵢⱼₖ ∂Fₖ/∂xⱼ.
∂ᵢεᵢⱼₖ∂ⱼFₖ contracts the antisymmetric εᵢⱼₖ with the symmetric ∂ᵢ∂ⱼ, giving 0 (for twice continuously differentiable F).

cards.f: Laplacian of a radial function in R³
cards.b: ∇²f(r) = (1/r²) d(r² df/dr)/dr = f″ + (2/r)f′.
∫_V ∇·F dV = ∫_S F·dS, for F continuously differentiable on V, a bounded region whose closed, piecewise smooth boundary S has the outward normal.
∫_S (∇ × F)·dS = ∮_C F·dr, for F continuously differentiable on the oriented, piecewise smooth surface S, with boundary C oriented by the right-hand rule relative to the normal.
∮_C (P dx + Q dy) = ∬_A (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dx dy, C anticlockwise round A.
∫_V (φ∇²ψ − ψ∇²φ) dV = ∫_S (φ∇ψ − ψ∇φ)·dS.

cards.f: Area enclosed by a plane curve C via Green
cards.b: (1/2)∮_C (x dy − y dx), C anticlockwise. For an ellipse it gives πab.
∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J = 0, from conserving ρ in every fixed volume and the divergence theorem (J = ρu for a fluid).
∇·E = ρ/ε₀, ∇·B = 0, ∇ × E = −∂B/∂t, ∇ × B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t.

cards.f: ∫_S r·dS for a closed surface S bounding V
cards.b: 3 × volume of V, since ∇·r = 3.
In R³: φ = A + B/r. In R² (or cylindrical symmetry): φ = A + B ln ρ.
Dirichlet data (φ on S): unique. Neumann data (∂φ/∂n on S): unique up to an additive constant.

cards.f: Key identity in the uniqueness proof
cards.b: ∫_V |∇ψ|² dV = ∫_S ψ ∂ψ/∂n dS for harmonic ψ (divergence theorem applied to ψ∇ψ).
A function harmonic in a bounded region and continuous up to the boundary attains its max and min on the boundary (on a connected region, not inside unless constant).

cards.f: Gauss's method for a spherically symmetric mass
cards.b: 4πr² g(r) = −4πG M(r), so g = −G M(r)/r² r̂, with M(r) the mass inside radius r.
φ(r) = −(1/4π) ∫ f(r′)/|r − r′| dV′ (for f decaying suitably).

cards.f: Field inside a uniform ball (density ρ₀)
cards.b: g = −(4/3)πGρ₀ r r̂: proportional to the distance from the centre.

cards.f: Transformation law for a rank-2 tensor
cards.b: T′ᵢⱼ = RᵢₖRⱼₗTₖₗ, where x′ᵢ = Rᵢⱼxⱼ and R is orthogonal.
Rank 2: λδᵢⱼ. Rank 3: λεᵢⱼₖ.
Setting two indices equal and summing lowers the rank by 2, e.g. the trace Tᵢᵢ is a scalar.

cards.f: ∫ xᵢxⱼ dV over the ball r ≤ a
cards.b: (4πa⁵/15)δᵢⱼ, by isotropy and taking the trace (∫ r² dV = 4πa⁵/5).
Iᵢⱼ = ∫ ρ(r²δᵢⱼ − xᵢxⱼ) dV; Lᵢ = Iᵢⱼωⱼ. Uniform sphere: (2/5)Ma²δᵢⱼ.
If Tᵢⱼvⱼ is a vector for every vector v, then Tᵢⱼ is a rank-2 tensor.

cards.f: Antisymmetric rank-2 tensor and a vector
cards.b: Aᵢⱼ = εᵢⱼₖωₖ, with ωₖ = (1/2)εₖᵢⱼAᵢⱼ.

questions.q: What is the curvature of the helix r(t) = (2 cos t, 2 sin t, t)?
questions.why: With a = 2, b = 1, κ = a/(a² + b²) = 2/5. 1/2 is the curvature of the circle of radius 2 (ignoring the climb); 1/5 = b/(a² + b²) is the torsion; and 2/√5 is |r′ × r″|/|r′|² (here |r′ × r″| = 2√5 and |r′| = √5), which divides by |r′|² instead of |r′|³.

questions.q: Which statement about a regular curve is correct?
options: The torsion is zero at every point if the curve lies in a plane
The curvature of a straight line is 1
The unit tangent is always parallel to its derivative dt̂/ds
The binormal is defined as t̂ + n̂
questions.why: A plane curve keeps the same binormal (normal to its plane), so db̂/ds = 0 and τ = 0. A straight line has κ = 0, not 1; dt̂/ds is perpendicular to t̂ because t̂ has constant length; and the binormal is the cross product t̂ × n̂, not a sum.

questions.q: For the helix r(t) = (3 cos t, 3 sin t, 4t), find the arc length s(t) from t = 0, the unit tangent t̂, the curvature κ and the torsion τ.
markScheme: t̂ = (−3 sin t, 3 cos t, 4)/5
dt̂/ds = (−3 cos t, −3 sin t, 0)/25, so κ = 3/25 and n̂ = (−cos t, −sin t, 0)
b̂ = (4 sin t, −4 cos t, 3)/5
questions.modelAnswer: r′ = (−3 sin t, 3 cos t, 4), |r′| = √(9 + 16) = 5, so s = 5t. t̂ = r′/5 = (−3 sin t, 3 cos t, 4)/5. dt̂/ds = (1/5)dt̂/dt = (−3 cos t, −3 sin t, 0)/25, so κ = 3/25 and n̂ = (−cos t, −sin t, 0). Then b̂ = t̂ × n̂ = (4 sin t, −4 cos t, 3)/5, and db̂/ds = (1/5)(4 cos t, 4 sin t, 0)/5 = −(4/25)n̂. With db̂/ds = −τn̂, τ = 4/25.

questions.q: F = (xy, x, 0). What is ∫ F·dr along r(t) = (t, t², 0) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1?
questions.why: F·r′ = (t·t²)(1) + (t)(2t) = t³ + 2t², which integrates to 1/4 + 2/3 = 11/12. 5/6 is the integral along the straight line (t, t, 0), a different path, showing F is not conservative; 7/12 = 1/4 + 1/3 forgets the factor 2 from dy = 2t dt; and 1 comes from mixing the two paths: taking xy = t² as on the straight line while using dy = 2t dt from the parabola (t² + 2t² integrates to 1).

questions.q: Which field is conservative on all of R³?
questions.why: (2xy + z, x², x) has zero curl and potential x²y + xz. (−y, x, 0) has curl (0, 0, 2); (xy, x, 0) has curl (0, 0, 1 − x); and (z, 0, −x) has curl (0, 2, 0). A non-zero curl rules out a potential.

questions.q: Show that F = (2xy + z, x², x) is conservative on R³, find a potential φ with F = ∇φ, and evaluate ∫_C F·dr for any path C from (0, 0, 0) to (1, 2, 3).
markScheme: Notes R³ is simply connected (or simply exhibits φ)
Integrates to φ = x²y + xz + constant, checking all three components
Answer 5
questions.modelAnswer: ∇ × F = (∂(x)/∂y − ∂(x²)/∂z, ∂(2xy + z)/∂z − ∂(x)/∂x, ∂(x²)/∂x − ∂(2xy + z)/∂y) = (0, 1 − 1, 2x − 2x) = 0. As R³ is simply connected, F is conservative. Integrating ∂φ/∂x = 2xy + z gives φ = x²y + xz + g(y, z); then ∂φ/∂y = x² + g_y = x² so g_y = 0, and ∂φ/∂z = x + g_z = x so g_z = 0. Hence φ = x²y + xz (+ constant). The integral is path independent and equals φ(1, 2, 3) − φ(0, 0, 0) = (1 × 2 + 1 × 3) − 0 = 5.

questions.q: In spherical polar coordinates (r, θ, φ), what is the volume element dV?
options: r² sin θ dr dθ dφ
r sin θ dr dθ dφ
r² cos θ dr dθ dφ
questions.why: The Jacobian of (r, θ, φ) ↦ (r sin θ cos φ, r sin θ sin φ, r cos θ) is r² sin θ. r sin θ has only one power of r (r sin θ dφ is the arc length round a circle of latitude); r² cos θ uses latitude rather than the polar angle; and r dr dθ dφ mixes up the plane polar element r dr dθ.

questions.q: What is the outward flux of F = (0, 0, z) through the curved surface of the hemisphere x² + y² + z² = a², z ≥ 0?
questions.why: On the sphere F·n̂ = z·(z/a) = a cos²θ, and ∫∫ a cos²θ a² sin θ dθ dφ over 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2 is 2πa³/3. This matches the divergence theorem (∇·F = 1, hemisphere volume 2πa³/3, zero flux through the base). 4πa³/3 is the volume of the whole ball; 2πa³ comes from taking F·n̂ = a everywhere, i.e. dropping the cos²θ factor; and 0 would need F to be tangential to the surface.

questions.q: Derive the Jacobian for spherical polar coordinates and use it to find the height of the centroid of a uniform solid hemisphere r ≤ a, z ≥ 0.
markScheme: Writes x, y, z in terms of r, θ, φ and the 3 × 3 matrix of partial derivatives
Evaluates the determinant as r² sin θ
Sets up ∫ z dV = ∫∫∫ r cos θ · r² sin θ dr dθ dφ with θ from 0 to π/2
Evaluates it as πa⁴/4
Divides by 2πa³/3 to get 3a/8
questions.modelAnswer: x = r sin θ cos φ, y = r sin θ sin φ, z = r cos θ. The Jacobian matrix has rows (sin θ cos φ, r cos θ cos φ, −r sin θ sin φ), (sin θ sin φ, r cos θ sin φ, r sin θ cos φ), (cos θ, −r sin θ, 0). Expanding along the bottom row: cos θ(r² sin θ cos θ cos²φ + r² sin θ cos θ sin²φ) + r sin θ(r sin²θ cos²φ + r sin²θ sin²φ) = r² sin θ cos²θ + r² sin³θ = r² sin θ. So dV = r² sin θ dr dθ dφ. Then ∫ z dV = ∫₀^a r³ dr × ∫₀^(π/2) sin θ cos θ dθ × ∫₀^(2π) dφ = (a⁴/4)(1/2)(2π) = πa⁴/4. The volume is 2πa³/3, so the centroid height is (πa⁴/4)/(2πa³/3) = 3a/8.

questions.q: For f = x²y + z³, what is the rate of change of f at (1, 2, −1) in the direction of (2, −1, 2)?
questions.why: ∇f = (2xy, x², 3z²) = (4, 1, 3) at the point, and the unit direction is (2, −1, 2)/3, giving (8 − 1 + 6)/3 = 13/3. 13 forgets to divide by |(2, −1, 2)| = 3; 5 drops the minus sign in the direction's y-component, giving (8 + 1 + 6)/3; 1/3 wrongly evaluates 3z² as −3 at z = −1.

questions.q: Which identity is correct for smooth fields?
questions.why: The curl of curl identity follows from εᵢⱼₖεₖₗₘ = δᵢₗδⱼₘ − δᵢₘδⱼₗ. The divergence of a cross product is G·(∇ × F) − F·(∇ × G), so the version given has the opposite sign; the product rule for curl has + ∇f × F; and ∇·(∇ × F) is always 0, a scalar, while ∇²F is a vector.

questions.q: Using suffix notation, prove that ∇·(F × G) = G·(∇ × F) − F·(∇ × G), and deduce that ∇·(∇f × ∇g) = 0 for smooth scalar fields f, g.
markScheme: Writes (F × G)ᵢ = εᵢⱼₖFⱼGₖ and applies ∂ᵢ with the product rule
Rearranges εᵢⱼₖ cyclically/anti-cyclically to identify Gₖ(∇ × F)ₖ
Identifies −Fⱼ(∇ × G)ⱼ with correct sign
Uses ∇ × ∇f = 0 and ∇ × ∇g = 0
Concludes the divergence is 0
questions.modelAnswer: ∇·(F × G) = ∂ᵢ(εᵢⱼₖFⱼGₖ) = εᵢⱼₖ(∂ᵢFⱼ)Gₖ + εᵢⱼₖFⱼ(∂ᵢGₖ). In the first term εᵢⱼₖ = εₖᵢⱼ, so it is Gₖ εₖᵢⱼ∂ᵢFⱼ = Gₖ(∇ × F)ₖ = G·(∇ × F). In the second, εᵢⱼₖ = −εⱼᵢₖ, so it is −Fⱼ εⱼᵢₖ∂ᵢGₖ = −F·(∇ × G). Hence the identity. With F = ∇f and G = ∇g, both curls vanish (∇ × ∇f = 0 since εᵢⱼₖ∂ⱼ∂ₖf = 0 by symmetry of mixed partials), so ∇·(∇f × ∇g) = 0.

questions.q: F = (−y, x, 0). What is ∮ F·dr round the circle x² + y² = a², z = 0, traversed anticlockwise when viewed from above?
questions.why: By Stokes's theorem with ∇ × F = (0, 0, 2) over the disc of area πa², the circulation is 2πa² (directly: ∫(a² sin²t + a² cos²t) dt = 2πa²). πa² forgets the factor 2 in the curl; 0 would hold only for an irrotational field; and 4πa² multiplies the curl component 2 by 2πa², the curved area of a hemisphere, instead of by the area πa² of the flat disc bounded by the circle.

questions.q: Which pair of Maxwell's equations implies the charge conservation equation ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J = 0?
questions.why: Taking the divergence of the Ampère–Maxwell law gives 0 = μ₀∇·J + μ₀ε₀ ∂(∇·E)/∂t, and Gauss's law turns ∇·E into ρ/ε₀. The other pairs never involve J and ρ together in a way that gives conservation: ∇·B = 0 with Faraday's law only gives ∂(∇·B)/∂t = 0, and the two divergence laws alone have no time derivative linking ρ to J.

questions.q: State Green's theorem in the plane, and use it to show that the area enclosed by the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 is πab.
markScheme: Correct statement with anticlockwise orientation
Chooses P = −y/2, Q = x/2 (or equivalent) so ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 1
Parametrises x = a cos t, y = b sin t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π
Evaluates (1/2)∫ (ab cos²t + ab sin²t) dt = πab
questions.modelAnswer: Green's theorem: if C is a simple closed curve traversed anticlockwise, enclosing the region A, and P, Q have continuous partial derivatives, then ∮_C (P dx + Q dy) = ∬_A (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dx dy. Take P = −y/2, Q = x/2; then ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 1, so the area is (1/2)∮(x dy − y dx). On the ellipse, x = a cos t, y = b sin t, dx = −a sin t dt, dy = b cos t dt, so x dy − y dx = ab(cos²t + sin²t) dt = ab dt. The area is (1/2) × ab × 2π = πab.

questions.q: φ satisfies Laplace's equation in a < r < b and depends only on r, with φ(a) = V and φ(b) = 0. What is φ?
questions.why: Radial harmonic functions in R³ are A + B/r, and fitting the boundary values gives Va(b − r)/(r(b − a)). V(b − r)/(b − a) is linear in r, which is harmonic only in one dimension; the logarithmic form is the cylindrically symmetric (two-dimensional) solution; and Va/r has the right value at r = a but is not zero at r = b.

questions.q: Which statement about the Neumann problem ∇²φ = f in V, ∂φ/∂n = g on S, is correct?
options: Any solution is unique up to adding a constant
There are always infinitely many essentially different solutions
It has a solution for every choice of f and g
questions.why: If φ₁ and φ₂ both solve it, ψ = φ₁ − φ₂ has ∫|∇ψ|² dV = 0, so ψ is constant: unique up to a constant. It is not strictly unique, because adding a constant keeps both equation and boundary data. The solutions do not differ by more than a constant. And a solution exists only if ∫_V f dV = ∫_S g dS, by the divergence theorem, so not for every f and g.

questions.q: Prove that the solution of Poisson's equation ∇²φ = f in a bounded region V, with φ = h prescribed on the boundary S, is unique.
markScheme: Considers ψ = φ₁ − φ₂, with ∇²ψ = 0 in V and ψ = 0 on S
Uses ∇·(ψ∇ψ) = |∇ψ|² + ψ∇²ψ
Applies the divergence theorem: ∫_V |∇ψ|² dV = ∫_S ψ ∇ψ·dS = 0
Deduces ∇ψ = 0 (non-negative continuous integrand), so ψ is constant
Boundary value 0 gives ψ ≡ 0, so φ₁ = φ₂
questions.modelAnswer: Suppose φ₁ and φ₂ are both solutions and let ψ = φ₁ − φ₂. Then ∇²ψ = f − f = 0 in V and ψ = h − h = 0 on S. Now ∇·(ψ∇ψ) = ∇ψ·∇ψ + ψ∇²ψ = |∇ψ|². By the divergence theorem, ∫_V |∇ψ|² dV = ∫_S ψ∇ψ·dS = 0, since ψ = 0 on S. The integrand is continuous and non-negative, so ∇ψ = 0 throughout V, and ψ is constant (V connected). Since ψ = 0 on S, the constant is 0. Therefore φ₁ = φ₂.

questions.q: Which of the following is an isotropic rank-2 tensor in R³?
options: nᵢnⱼ for a fixed unit vector n
questions.why: Any multiple of δᵢⱼ is unchanged by rotations, and these are the only isotropic rank-2 tensors. δᵢⱼ + xᵢxⱼ depends on position and picks out the direction of x; εᵢⱼ₃ picks out the third axis, so its components change under rotations about other axes; and nᵢnⱼ singles out the direction n.

questions.q: If Tᵢⱼ is a rank-2 tensor and v is a vector, what is Tᵢⱼvᵢvⱼ?
questions.why: The product Tᵢⱼvₖvₗ has rank 4, and the two contractions (k = i and l = j) each lower the rank by 2, leaving rank 0, a scalar. A vector would need one free index; a rank-2 tensor two free indices; and rank 4 is the product before contracting.

questions.q: Using isotropy, evaluate ∫ xᵢxⱼ dV over the ball r ≤ a. Hence show that the inertia tensor of a uniform solid sphere of mass M and radius a about its centre is (2/5)Ma²δᵢⱼ.
markScheme: Argues the integral is an isotropic rank-2 tensor (ball invariant under rotations), so equals λδᵢⱼ
Takes the trace: 3λ = ∫ r² dV = ∫ r² · 4πr² dr = 4πa⁵/5
λ = 4πa⁵/15
Uses Iᵢⱼ = ρ∫(r²δᵢⱼ − xᵢxⱼ) dV = ρ(4πa⁵/5 − 4πa⁵/15)δᵢⱼ = (8πρa⁵/15)δᵢⱼ
With M = (4/3)πa³ρ, gives (2/5)Ma²δᵢⱼ
questions.modelAnswer: Let Kᵢⱼ = ∫ xᵢxⱼ dV over the ball. Under a rotation x′ = Rx the ball maps to itself, so K′ᵢⱼ = RᵢₖRⱼₗKₖₗ = Kᵢⱼ: K is isotropic and hence K = λδᵢⱼ. Taking the trace: 3λ = ∫ r² dV = ∫₀^a r² · 4πr² dr = 4πa⁵/5, so λ = 4πa⁵/15. For a uniform sphere of density ρ, Iᵢⱼ = ρ∫(r²δᵢⱼ − xᵢxⱼ) dV = ρ(4πa⁵/5 − 4πa⁵/15)δᵢⱼ = (8πρa⁵/15)δᵢⱼ. With M = (4/3)πa³ρ, (2/5)Ma² = (2/5)(4/3)πρa⁵ = 8πρa⁵/15. So Iᵢⱼ = (2/5)Ma²δᵢⱼ: every axis through the centre is a principal axis with moment (2/5)Ma².

questions.q:
(a) State Stokes's theorem and the divergence theorem, including the conditions on orientation. [4]
(b) Let F = (−y³, x³, z) and let S be the hemisphere x² + y² + z² = a², z ≥ 0, with upward normal. Verify Stokes's theorem by computing ∫_S (∇ × F)·dS directly and ∮_C F·dr round the boundary circle. [10]
(c) Show that if S is any closed surface bounding a volume V, then ∫_S r·dS = 3V. Taking the divergence of the Ampère–Maxwell equation ∇ × B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t and using ∇·E = ρ/ε₀, derive the equation of charge conservation and explain its integral meaning. [6]
markScheme: (a) Correct statements: right-hand rule linking C and normal; outward normal for the closed surface
(b) Surface integral set up with dS = a² sin θ r̂ dθ dφ, (∇ × F)·r̂ = 3a² sin²θ cos θ
(b) Evaluates 6πa⁴ ∫ sin³θ cos θ dθ = 3πa⁴/2
(b) Line integral a⁴∫(sin⁴t + cos⁴t) dt = 3πa⁴/2, with anticlockwise orientation consistent with the upward normal
(c) ∇·r = 3 and the divergence theorem give 3V
(c) Integral form: rate of decrease of charge in V equals the current out through S
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Stokes: if S is a piecewise smooth oriented surface with boundary curve C, oriented so that C is traversed anticlockwise when viewed from the side the normal points to (right-hand rule), and F is continuously differentiable, then ∫_S (∇ × F)·dS = ∮_C F·dr. Divergence theorem: if V is a bounded region with piecewise smooth closed boundary S and outward normal, and F is continuously differentiable on V and S, ∫_V ∇·F dV = ∫_S F·dS.

(b) ∇ × F = (∂z/∂y − ∂(x³)/∂z, ∂(−y³)/∂z − ∂z/∂x, ∂(x³)/∂x − ∂(−y³)/∂y) = (0, 0, 3x² + 3y²). On the sphere r = a, dS = r̂ a² sin θ dθ dφ, and (∇ × F)·r̂ = 3(x² + y²)(z/a) = 3a² sin²θ cos θ. So ∫_S (∇ × F)·dS = ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀^(π/2) 3a² sin²θ cos θ · a² sin θ dθ dφ = 6πa⁴ ∫₀^(π/2) sin³θ cos θ dθ = 6πa⁴ × [sin⁴θ/4] = 6πa⁴/4 = 3πa⁴/2.
The boundary is the circle x = a cos t, y = a sin t, z = 0; with an upward normal it is traversed anticlockwise (t increasing). F·r′ = (−a³ sin³t)(−a sin t) + (a³ cos³t)(a cos t) = a⁴(sin⁴t + cos⁴t). Since ∫₀^(2π) sin⁴t dt = ∫₀^(2π) cos⁴t dt = 3π/4, the line integral is a⁴ × 3π/2 = 3πa⁴/2. The two sides agree, verifying Stokes's theorem. (As a check, the flat disc gives ∫∫ 3ρ² ρ dρ dφ = 3πa⁴/2 too.)

(c) ∇·r = ∂x/∂x + ∂y/∂y + ∂z/∂z = 3, so by the divergence theorem ∫_S r·dS = ∫_V 3 dV = 3V. Taking the divergence of the Ampère–Maxwell law: ∇·(∇ × B) = 0 for any smooth B, so 0 = μ₀∇·J + μ₀ε₀ ∂(∇·E)/∂t = μ₀∇·J + μ₀ ∂ρ/∂t. Hence ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J = 0. Integrating over a fixed volume V and using the divergence theorem: d/dt ∫_V ρ dV = −∫_S J·dS. The charge in V changes only because of current flowing through its boundary, so charge is neither created nor destroyed.

questions.q:
(a) Show that the only solutions of Laplace's equation in R³ ∖ {0} that depend only on r = |r| are φ = A + B/r. Find the solution in a < r < b with φ = V on r = a and φ = 0 on r = b. [6]
(b) The gravitational potential satisfies ∇²φ = 4πGρ, with g = −∇φ. A planet occupies r ≤ a and has density ρ = ρ₀r/a. Use Gauss's method to find g everywhere, and find φ everywhere, taking φ → 0 as r → ∞ and φ continuous at r = a. [10]
(c) Quoting a uniqueness theorem, explain why your answer in (a) is the only solution of the boundary value problem, even without assuming spherical symmetry. [4]
markScheme: (a) Radial Laplacian (1/r²)(r²φ′)′ = 0 integrated twice to A + B/r
(a) Boundary conditions give φ = Va(b − r)/(r(b − a))
(b) Divergence theorem on a sphere of radius r: 4πr²g(r) = −4πG M(r) with g = g(r) r̂
(b) M(r) = πρ₀r⁴/a for r ≤ a; total mass M = πρ₀a³
(b) g = −(πGρ₀r²/a) r̂ inside and −(πGρ₀a³/r²) r̂ outside
(b) φ = −πGρ₀a³/r outside; inside φ = πGρ₀(r³/(3a) − 4a²/3)
(c) Dirichlet uniqueness: same boundary data and same equation give the same solution, so the symmetric solution is the solution
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For φ = φ(r), ∇²φ = (1/r²) d(r² dφ/dr)/dr. Setting this to zero, r² dφ/dr = −B (constant), so dφ/dr = −B/r² and φ = A + B/r. Every such function is harmonic for r ≠ 0, so these are exactly the radial solutions. Boundary conditions: A + B/a = V and A + B/b = 0. Subtracting, B(1/a − 1/b) = V, so B = Vab/(b − a) and A = −Va/(b − a). Hence φ = Va(b − r)/(r(b − a)).

(b) By symmetry g = g(r) r̂. Integrating ∇²φ = 4πGρ over the ball of radius r and using the divergence theorem: ∫_S ∇φ·dS = 4πG M(r), i.e. −4πr²g(r) = 4πG M(r), so g(r) = −G M(r)/r².
For r ≤ a: M(r) = ∫₀^r (ρ₀s/a) 4πs² ds = πρ₀r⁴/a. So g = −(πGρ₀r²/a) r̂. The total mass is M = πρ₀a³, so for r ≥ a, g = −(πGρ₀a³/r²) r̂ = −(GM/r²) r̂.
Potential: dφ/dr = −g(r) = G M(r)/r². Outside, φ = −GM/r = −πGρ₀a³/r, which tends to 0 at infinity. Inside, dφ/dr = πGρ₀r²/a, so φ = πGρ₀r³/(3a) + C. Continuity at r = a: πGρ₀a²/3 + C = −πGρ₀a², so C = −4πGρ₀a²/3. Hence φ = πGρ₀(r³/(3a) − 4a²/3) for r ≤ a. Check: (1/r²)(r² × πGρ₀r²/a)′ = (1/r²)(4πGρ₀r³/a) = 4πGρ₀r/a = 4πGρ, as required.

(c) Uniqueness theorem: the solution of ∇²φ = f in a bounded region V with φ prescribed on the whole boundary S is unique. (Proof: the difference ψ of two solutions is harmonic with ψ = 0 on S, and ∫_V |∇ψ|² dV = ∫_S ψ ∂ψ/∂n dS = 0 forces ψ ≡ 0.) The shell a < r < b is bounded with boundary the two spheres. The function in (a) satisfies Laplace's equation there and the boundary data on both spheres. Any other solution, symmetric or not, would have the same boundary values, so by uniqueness it equals the one found. Thus guessing a symmetric solution is a legitimate method.
